# Summary

How well can information available at enrollment predict whether a student will drop out, still be studying, or graduate by the end of their program’s normal duration? We studied 4,424 students at one Portuguese institution. On the 885 students held out for testing, logistic regression with five enrollment predictors scored 0.509 on  macro F1, which balances precision and recall within each outcome and gives all three outcomes equal weight. Always predicting graduation scored 0.222. The model identified 145 of the 284 students who dropped out. Using its predictions alone to decide whom to contact would therefore miss nearly half the students an adviser hoped to reach.

# Introduction

An academic adviser meets a new student before the student has taken a course or earned a semester grade. At that point, the institution already knows the program the student entered, how they applied and their admission grade. If these details help distinguish later academic outcomes, they could inform which students are offered an early conversation about support. A missed dropout could mean a missed opportunity for outreach. Equally, a student who needs longer to finish could be misidentified as having left.

**Using information available at enrollment, how well can we predict whether a student will have dropped out, still be enrolled, or have graduated by the end of their program’s normal duration?**

We use the public *Predict Students’ Dropout and Academic Success* dataset. Each of the 4,424 rows represents one undergraduate student at the Polytechnic Institute of Portalegre in Portugal, across 17 programs. The source records 36 predictors covering prior education, demographics, socioeconomic conditions and academic performance. The target is their recorded academic status at the end of the program’s normal duration. A student labeled *Enrolled* was still studying at that cutoff and could graduate later. The source also contains academic performance recorded at the end of each of the first two semesters. This distinction between entry information and later observations determines which variables are eligible for an enrollment-time prediction. [1](#ref-data), [2](#ref-paper)

# Methods

## Data acquisition and computational setup

We used Python for the analysis, pandas to organize the records, scikit-learn to partition the data, and Matplotlib to draw the figures. The code downloads the original archive from the University of California, Irvine (UCI) Machine Learning Repository, saves its CSV file in the project’s raw-data directory and reads its semicolon-delimited fields. [1](#ref-data)

## Training and test split

We first split the 4,424 raw records into 80% training and 20% test data, stratifying by outcome so both partitions retain similar class proportions. A fixed random seed reproduces the split. We then removed the 12 semester-performance columns from both partitions and trimmed whitespace from the column names. This left 24 candidate predictors and the target. We saved the processed partitions separately. All exploratory comparisons below use the training partition.

```{python}
train, test = train_test_split(
    students,
    test_size=0.20,
    random_state=522,
    stratify=students["Target"],
)

semester_columns = train.columns[
    train.columns.str.startswith(("Curricular units 1st sem", "Curricular units 2nd sem"))
]
train = train.drop(columns=semester_columns).rename(columns=str.strip)
test = test.drop(columns=semester_columns).rename(columns=str.strip)

processed_dir = project_root / "data" / "processed"
processed_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

train.to_csv(processed_dir / "train.csv", index=False)
test.to_csv(processed_dir / "test.csv", index=False)
```

## Exploratory analysis

We counted outcomes, checked missing values and duplicate records, and used the source dictionary to interpret numeric category codes. Most students enrolled in their late teens or early twenties. The median age was 20 years, but a few much older entrants, with ages reaching 70, pulled the mean up to 23.1 years. We therefore report the median, which describes the middle student and is less sensitive to extreme ages. For both age and admission grade, we compare each outcome group's median and interquartile range (the middle 50% of students). For application route, program and financial status, we calculated percentages within each subgroup and reported its size. This matters because program enrollments range from eight to several hundred training students. We used these comparisons to propose features for classification. [1](#ref-data)

```{python}
from io import StringIO
from xml.etree import ElementTree as ET

def add_tip(artist, details, text):
    """Associate one plotted mark with its tooltip text."""
    key = f"mark-{len(details)}"
    artist.set_gid(key)
    details[key] = text

def display_interactive_figure(fig, details, description):
    """Embed the figure and its tooltips directly in the HTML report."""
    buffer = StringIO()
    with plt.rc_context({"svg.fonttype": "none"}):
        fig.savefig(buffer, format="svg", bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)
    ns = "http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"
    ET.register_namespace("", ns)
    ET.register_namespace("xlink", "http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink")
    svg = ET.fromstring(buffer.getvalue())
    svg.attrib.update({"role": "group", "aria-label": description})
    seen = set()
    for group in svg.iter(f"{{{ns}}}g"):
        key = group.attrib.pop("id", None)
        if key in details:
            text = details[key]
            group.attrib.update({"class": "chart-mark", "role": "img", "aria-label": text,
                                 "tabindex": "-1" if text in seen else "0"})
            seen.add(text)
    markup = ET.tostring(svg, encoding="unicode")
    display(HTML('<div class="interactive-figure">' + markup + """
      <span class="chart-tooltip" aria-hidden="true" hidden></span>
      <style>
        .interactive-figure svg { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }
        .interactive-figure svg text { pointer-events: none; }
        .interactive-figure .chart-mark { cursor: help; }
        .interactive-figure .chart-mark:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid #23547d; }
        .chart-tooltip { position: fixed; z-index: 1000; pointer-events: none;
          max-width: min(22rem, 90vw); padding: .4rem .65rem; background: #172735;
          color: white; border-radius: .3rem; font: 0.9rem/1.4 system-ui; }
      </style>
      <script>
        (() => {
          const chart = document.currentScript.parentElement;
          const tip = chart.querySelector(".chart-tooltip");
          function show(event) {
            const mark = event.target.closest(".chart-mark");
            if (!mark) { tip.hidden = true; return; }
            const box = mark.getBoundingClientRect();
            const x = event.clientX ?? (box.left + box.width / 2);
            const y = event.clientY ?? (box.top + box.height / 2);
            tip.textContent = mark.getAttribute("aria-label");
            tip.hidden = false;
            tip.style.left = Math.max(4, Math.min(x + 12, innerWidth - tip.offsetWidth - 4)) + "px";
            tip.style.top = (y + 14 + tip.offsetHeight < innerHeight
              ? y + 14 : Math.max(4, y - tip.offsetHeight - 8)) + "px";
          }
          for (const event of ["pointerover", "pointermove", "click", "focusin"])
            chart.addEventListener(event, show);
          for (const event of ["pointerleave", "focusout"])
            chart.addEventListener(event, () => { tip.hidden = true; });
          chart.addEventListener("keydown", event => {
            if (event.key === "Escape") tip.hidden = true;
          });
          document.addEventListener("pointerdown", event => {
            if (!chart.contains(event.target)) tip.hidden = true;
          });
        })();
      </script>
    </div>"""))

eda = train
classes = ["Dropout", "Enrolled", "Graduate"]
colors = ["#AD4824", "#49658D", "#167361"]

def outcome_mix(groups, outcomes):
    counts = pd.crosstab(groups, outcomes).reindex(columns=classes, fill_value=0)
    sizes = counts.sum(axis=1)
    percentages = counts.div(sizes, axis=0).mul(100)
    return percentages.assign(Students=sizes)
```

## Model and evaluation

### Predictor selection and preprocessing

We selected five predictors based on enrollment timing and the comparisons in the training data. Program and application route capture differences in how students enter higher education. Age and admission grade allow the model to examine differences among students who enter through the same route. We also included the scholarship indicator, assuming it reflects the student's status at enrollment. We excluded debt and fee status because the dates of those records are uncertain.

For logistic regression, we use a separate indicator for each program and application route because their numeric codes identify categories. We standardize age and admission grade so their different units do not determine the strength of regularization. Scholarship status already uses a binary indicator. The preprocessor is defined here for use inside the model pipeline, where it can learn categories, means, and standard deviations using only the training portion of each cross-validation fold. [3](#ref-validation)

```{python}
categorical_features = ["Course", "Application mode"]
numeric_features = ["Age at enrollment", "Admission grade"]
binary_features = ["Scholarship holder"]
predictors = categorical_features + numeric_features + binary_features

X_train, y_train = train[predictors], train["Target"]
X_test, y_test = test[predictors], test["Target"]

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer([
    ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical_features),
    ("numeric", StandardScaler(), numeric_features),
    ("binary", "passthrough", binary_features),
])
```

### Classifiers, tuning and evaluation

We selected a logistic regression classifier as our model for this problem as it natively models all three outcomes, has interpretable coefficients, and is less likely to overfit with only five predictors. We chose to compare the performance of the logistic regression classifier with a baseline model which always predicts the most common class, in this case being Graduate. Each of the baseline model and the logistic regression classifier are passed through a pipeline which includes the pre-processing. Then, cross-validation is completed on training data with 5 folds. This allows us to compare a logistic regression classifier with the baseline model without evaluating on the test set, and shows how metrics change between samples of students. We can progress to tuning the model now that we have a baseline model and a default logistic regression classifier cross-validated.

We use F1 to evaluate the models since the classes are unbalanced, and using accuracy alone would be misleading when comparing with the baseline. Macro F1 was used to average the class-specific scores since it gives equal weight to each class. In our problem, the models ability to predict each class is important so using macro F1 is fitting. [4](#ref-f1) The model was tuned using a grid search with 5-fold cross validation since we only had 2 hyper-parameters to tune: C (regularization, 0.001-100), and class weighting. The model with hyper-parameters which optimize the macro F1 score is selected. The test set was held out for the entirety of the model building process, and after the model is finalized, it is refit (during grid search automatically) on all of the training data and evaluated using the test data.

**Table 1. Size and completeness of the training data. The last two rows count explicit “unknown” codes in the source data dictionary.**

```{python}
profile = pd.DataFrame({

    ],
```

Table 1 shows why a simple missing-value check tells only part of the story. All cells have a recorded value, yet for 101 students the value for maternal qualification explicitly means “unknown.” We retain this category. We also read program and application route codes as names of categories, since the distance between two codes has no academic interpretation.

Academic status at the end of the normal program duration. Each bar gives the percentage and number of students out of 3,539.

:::

Hover over a mark, tap it, or use the Tab key to read its exact values in any figure.

In @fig-outcomes, 1,767 students graduated, 1,137 dropped out and 635 were still enrolled. Always predicting graduation would get 49.9% of the training records right while missing every student who dropped out or remained enrolled. An adviser therefore needs information that helps distinguish all three groups. Admission grade and age are two natural places to start.

### Do admission grades or ages differ across the three outcomes?

::: {#fig-entry}


Age and admission grade by outcome. Dots mark medians and thick lines span the middle 50% of students. The colors follow the labeled rows in each panel, with orange for dropout, blue for continued enrollment and green for graduation.

:::

The median-and-interval plot (@fig-entry) shows where the middle half of each group falls. How far do ages and grades extend beyond that middle half?

::: {#fig-entry-box}

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.2, 3.3), layout="constrained")
details = {}
for ax, measure, label in zip(
    axes,
    ["Age at enrollment", "Admission grade"],
    ["Age at enrollment (years)", "Admission grade (points out of 200)"],
):
    samples = [eda.loc[eda["Target"].eq(outcome), measure] for outcome in classes]
    boxes = ax.boxplot(
        samples, orientation="horizontal", patch_artist=True, whis=1.5, widths=0.55,
        medianprops={"color": "black", "linewidth": 1.7},
        showfliers=False,  # Draw repeated outlying values once and report their frequency.
    )
    for i, (box, color, values) in enumerate(zip(boxes["boxes"], colors, samples)):
        outcome = classes[i]
        q1, median, q3 = values.quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
        whiskers = boxes["whiskers"][2*i:2*i+2]
        low, high = [line.get_xdata()[-1] for line in whiskers]
        text = (f"{outcome}, {label}. Median {median:g}. Middle 50% from {q1:g} to {q3:g}. "
                f"Whiskers from {low:g} to {high:g}. Group size {len(values):,}.")
        for artist in [box, boxes["medians"][i], *whiskers, *boxes["caps"][2*i:2*i+2]]:
            add_tip(artist, details, text)
        outside = values[(values < low) | (values > high)].value_counts().sort_index()
        for value, count in outside.items():
            point, = ax.plot(value, i + 1, "o", markersize=3, markerfacecolor="none",
                             markeredgecolor="black", alpha=0.5)
            noun = "student" if count == 1 else "students"
            add_tip(point, details, f"{outcome}, {label}. {value:g} ({count} {noun}).")
        box.set_facecolor(color)
        box.set_alpha(0.65)
    ax.set_yticks(range(1, len(classes) + 1), classes)
    ax.invert_yaxis()
    ax.set_xlabel(label)
    ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.2)
    ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
display_interactive_figure(fig, details, "All three outcome groups have older entrants beyond the upper age whisker. Admission grade boxes overlap across the three groups.")
```

Enrollment age and admission grade by outcome in the training set. The line inside each box is the median. Boxes span the middle 50%, and whiskers reach the most extreme observed values within 1.5 interquartile ranges of the box. Each point beyond a whisker marks a distinct observed value. Its tooltip gives the number of students at that value.

:::

In @fig-entry-box, older entrants appear beyond the upper age whisker in every outcome group. Even among graduates, whose median entry age was 19, the oldest entrant was 62. The admission grade boxes overlap substantially across all three outcomes.

The dropout and still-enrolled groups had the same median admission grade, **124.2 out of 200** (@fig-entry). Even the graduate median of 127.3 sits inside the middle half of the dropout group, which spans 115.2 to 133.8. A grade near 125 would therefore give the adviser little basis, on its own, for distinguishing these outcomes.

Age shows a clearer difference. The median entry ages were 23, 20 and 19 years for students who dropped out, remained enrolled and graduated, respectively. The middle half of the dropout group spanned ages 19 to 30, compared with 18 to 21 for graduates. This wider spread raises an important follow-up. One application route is specifically for applicants over 23, so its dropout share may partly reflect whom it admits.

### How does the difference between application routes change among older entrants?

::: {#fig-route}

```{python}
route_rows = []
for population, frame in [("All ages", eda), ("Age 24 and older", eda.loc[eda["Age at enrollment"] >= 24])]:
    is_over_23_route = frame["Application mode"].eq(39)
    for label, mask in [("Over-23 route", is_over_23_route), ("Other routes", ~is_over_23_route)]:
        outcomes = frame.loc[mask, "Target"]
        dropouts = outcomes.eq("Dropout").sum()
        route_rows.append([population, label, len(outcomes), dropouts, round(100 * dropouts / len(outcomes), 1)])

routes = pd.DataFrame(route_rows, columns=["Population", "Route", "Students", "Dropouts", "Share"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.2, 3.4), layout="constrained")
bar_details = {}
for offset, name, color in [(-0.18, "Over-23 route", "#325563"), (0.18, "Other routes", "#8495AA")]:
    group = routes[routes["Route"] == name]
    positions = [i + offset for i in range(len(group))]
    bars = ax.barh(positions, group["Share"], height=0.30, color=color, label=name)
    for bar, y, row in zip(bars, positions, group.itertuples()):
        key = f"route-{row.Index}"
        bar.set_gid(key)
        bar_details[key] = (
            f"{row.Population}, {name}. {row.Dropouts:,} of {row.Students:,} students "
            f"dropped out ({row.Share:.1f}%)."
        )
        ax.text(row.Share + 0.9, y, f"{row.Share:.1f}%  ({row.Students:,})", va="center", fontsize=10)
ax.set_yticks([0, 1], ["All ages", "Age 24 and older"])
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlim(0, 73)
ax.set_xticks([0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60])
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(100, decimals=0))
ax.set_xlabel("Share who dropped out within each group")
ax.legend(loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0, 1), frameon=False, ncol=2)
ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
display_interactive_figure(fig, bar_details, "Dropout shares by application route and age group.")
```

Dropout share within each application route, first across all ages and then among students aged 24 or older. Parentheses give the size of each group. The second comparison uses a subset of the first.

:::

Across all ages, 56.1% of students entering through the over-23 route dropped out, compared with 26.9% through other routes (@fig-route). But those two groups draw from different age ranges. All 631 students on the over-23 route were at least 24. When we apply the same age restriction to other routes, 375 students remain and their dropout share rises to 52.0%.

The observed gap falls from **29.2 to 4.1 percentage points**. That gives us a reason to test age and route together. Even within this age range, students can differ in exact age, program and other circumstances. Looking at program next also brings the students still enrolled back into view.


Percentage of students in each outcome within each program. Each row represents 100% of a program’s training students. Labels give the group size. Displayed percentages are rounded.

:::

Evening Management and Informatics Engineering look almost identical if we compare only dropout, at **53.8% and 53.2%** (@fig-programs). The difference emerges when we ask where the rest of their students were at the cutoff. In Informatics Engineering, 36.9% were still enrolled and 9.9% had graduated. In Evening Management, 21.0% were still enrolled and 25.2% had graduated. That distinction is precisely what the three-class prediction question preserves.

Nursing provides a useful reference, with 71.4% of 622 students graduating. At the other end of the figure, Biofuel Production Technologies has only eight training students. One student accounts for 12.5 percentage points there. Program is worth testing, but the smallest groups provide little evidence for a precise program-specific prediction. Program is recorded at entry. Financial records raise a different question about what was known at that point.

### Which financial differences are large enough to investigate, and when were they observable?

**Table 2. Academic outcomes within each recorded financial status. Each pair of rows describes the full training set. Percentages across a row may differ slightly from 100 because of rounding.**

```{python}
financial_tables = []
for column, labels in [
    ("Tuition fees up to date", {0: "Fees outstanding", 1: "Fees current"}),
    ("Debtor", {0: "No recorded debt", 1: "Recorded debt"}),
    ("Scholarship holder", {0: "No scholarship", 1: "Scholarship holder"}),
]:
    mix = outcome_mix(eda[column], eda["Target"]).rename(index=labels)
    financial_tables.append(mix)
financial = pd.concat(financial_tables)[["Students", *classes]].round(1)

financial.index.name = "Recorded status"
financial = financial.reset_index().rename(columns={
    "Dropout": "Dropped out (%)", "Enrolled": "Still enrolled (%)", "Graduate": "Graduated (%)"
})
display(HTML(financial.to_html(index=False, float_format=lambda x: f"{x:.1f}",
                               formatters={"Students": "{:,}".format})))
```

Table 2 shows that 88.2% of students with outstanding fees dropped out, compared with 24.7% of those whose fees were current. Reading across the scholarship rows reveals a different pattern. Graduation was recorded for 75.5% of scholarship holders and 41.4% of students without a scholarship. These comparisons describe associations. They cannot tell us whether paying fees or receiving a scholarship would change an individual student’s outcome.

For the adviser, the decisive question is **when the status was recorded**. A balance updated after a student left could make past dropout easy to recognize without helping predict it at enrollment. The file supplies no student-level date for these financial records. That is why a large difference can justify investigating a feature while still leaving it out of the initial model.

The training data suggest that program, application route, and age at enrollment are worth examining together. Students with different outcomes often had similar admission grades, so the value of grade alongside those other predictors remains a question for model validation. We included all four predictors in the model, along with scholarship status, which was known at enrollment. We excluded debt and tuition-payment status because we could not confirm when those values were recorded.

## Hyper-parameter tuning and cross-validation

We first compared different hyper parameters of C (regularization) and class weight on the logistic regression model. Table 3 shows the mean validation and training macro F1 scores for each combination of settings in the grid search.

**Table 3. Grid search results for Logistic Regression ordered by macro F1 across 5 CV folds.**

```{python}
# define cv
cv = 5

# helper function for cross validation
def mean_std_cross_val_scores(model, X, y, **kwargs):
  scores = pd.DataFrame(cross_validate(model, X, y, **kwargs))
  summary = pd.concat([
    scores.mean().add_suffix("_mean"),
    scores.std(ddof=0).add_suffix("_std")
  ])
  return summary

# chosen models, baseline and lr
models = {
  "Baseline (most frequent class)" : DummyClassifier(strategy = 'most_frequent'),
  "Logistic Regression (default param)" : LogisticRegression(max_iter = 1000)
}

# define and build results using preprocessor and helper function
results_dict = {}
for name, model in models.items():
  pipe = make_pipeline(preprocessor, model)
  results_dict[name] = mean_std_cross_val_scores(
    pipe, X_train, y_train, cv = cv, scoring = "f1_macro", return_train_score = True)
    
pipe = make_pipeline(preprocessor, models["Logistic Regression (default param)"])

# define hyperparameter's to try
param_grid = {
  'logisticregression__C' : [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100],
  'logisticregression__class_weight' : [None, "balanced"]
}

# only 2 hyperparameters so gridsearch, define
search = GridSearchCV(
  pipe,
  param_grid,
  cv = cv,
  scoring = "f1_macro",
  return_train_score = True
)

# fit the gridsearch to the training data
search.fit(X_train, y_train)

# create a results table, ranked by validation macro F1
results = pd.DataFrame(search.cv_results_)
cv_table = results[["rank_test_score", "param_logisticregression__C", 
"param_logisticregression__class_weight", "mean_test_score",
"std_test_score", "mean_train_score"]].rename(columns = {
  "rank_test_score" : "Rank",
  "param_logisticregression__C" : "C",
  "param_logisticregression__class_weight" : "Class Weight",
  "mean_test_score" : "Validation Macro F1",
  "std_test_score" : "Validation Std",
  "mean_train_score" : "Train Macro F1"
}).sort_values("Rank")
cv_table["Class Weight"] = cv_table["Class Weight"].fillna("none")

cv_table.style.format(precision = 3).hide(axis = "index")
```

Balanced class weights gave a greater average macro F1 for every value of C than the unweighted models. Scores were similar for all values of C with balanced class weights, except for the greatest regularization of 0.001. A combination of C = 0.01 with balanced class weights gives the best performance, achieving a validation macro F1 score of 0.522.

**Table 4. Cross-validation scores for the baseline and logistic regression models (base and tuned) on training data.**

```{python}
# add the tuned model to results_dict
results_dict["Logistic Regression (tuned)"] = mean_std_cross_val_scores(
  search.best_estimator_, X_train, y_train,
  cv = cv, scoring = "f1_macro", return_train_score = True
)

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results_dict).round(4).T[["test_score_mean", "test_score_std", "train_score_mean"]].rename(columns = {
  "test_score_mean" : "Validation macro F1",
  "test_score_std" : "Validation Std",
  "train_score_mean" : "Training macro F1"
})
results_df.style.format(precision = 3)
```

Table 4 compares the performance of the baseline model and the default and tuned logistic regression models. The baseline model, with most frequent class prediction, reached a macro F1 of 0.222. The un-tuned logistic regression model increased this to 0.471. Further tuning of regularization and class balance brought the macro F1 score of the model to 0.522.

## Held-out test performance

**Table 5. Test performance metrics for the baseline and tuned logistic regression model.**

```{python}
baseline = models["Baseline (most frequent class)"]
baseline.fit(X_train, y_train)
baseline_pred = baseline.predict(X_test)
lr_pred = search.best_estimator_.predict(X_test)

test_results = pd.DataFrame(
  {
    "Accuracy" : [
      accuracy_score(y_test, baseline_pred),
      accuracy_score(y_test, lr_pred)
    ],
    "Macro Precision" : [
      precision_score(y_test, baseline_pred, average = "macro", zero_division = 0),
      precision_score(y_test, lr_pred, average = "macro", zero_division = 0)
    ],
    "Macro Recall" : [
      recall_score(y_test, baseline_pred, average = "macro"),
      recall_score(y_test, lr_pred, average = "macro")
    ],
    "Macro F1" : [
      f1_score(y_test, baseline_pred, average = "macro"),
      f1_score(y_test, lr_pred, average = "macro")
    ]
  },
  index = ["Baseline (most frequent)", "Logistic Regression (tuned)"]
)

test_results.style.format(precision = 3)
```

Running the tuned model on the test data resulted in a macro F1 of 0.509, while the baseline model was 0.222 in Table 5. This result is close to the validation result of 0.522. The accuracy for the baseline model is 0.499 where the tuned logistic regression model achieved 0.546.

**Table 6. Test metrics for the tuned logistic regression model by class**

```{python}
report = classification_report(y_test, lr_pred, labels=["Dropout", "Enrolled", "Graduate"], output_dict = True)

per_class_results = pd.DataFrame(report).drop(columns = ["accuracy", "macro avg", "weighted avg"]).T.rename(columns = {
  "precision" : "Precision",
  "recall" : "Recall",
  "f1-score" : "F1",
  "support" : "# students"
  }
)
per_class_results["# students"] = per_class_results["# students"].astype(int)
per_class_results.style.format(precision=3)
```

```{python}
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

matrix = ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(
  y_test,
  lr_pred,
  labels = ["Dropout", "Enrolled", "Graduate"],
  cmap = "Blues"
)

fig = matrix.figure_
details = {}
for i, actual in enumerate(classes):
    total = matrix.confusion_matrix[i].sum()
    for j, predicted in enumerate(classes):
        count = matrix.confusion_matrix[i, j]
        cell = Rectangle((j - 0.5, i - 0.5), 1, 1, facecolor=(1, 1, 1, 0.001),
                         edgecolor="none", zorder=4)
        matrix.ax_.add_patch(cell)
        add_tip(cell, details, f"Actual {actual}, predicted {predicted}. {count} of "
                f"{total} students with actual outcome {actual} ({100 * count / total:.1f}%).")
display_interactive_figure(fig, details, "Confusion matrix for the tuned logistic regression model on the test students.")
```

Confusion matrix for the tuned logistic regression model on the test students.

:::

The performance of the tuned model differed by the three student outcomes as shown in Table 6. For students that graduated, the model performed the strongest achieving an F1 score of 0.663. The model performed worse for dropouts and enrolled students with F1 scores of 0.508 and 0.356, respectively. Of the 442 test students that graduated, the model identified 269 of them correctly. The confusion matrix in @fig-confusion shows where the errors were concentrated. Notably, 98 of the 442 test students that graduated were predicted as dropouts and 85 of test students that dropped out were classified as enrolled. The model was able to capture 145 of 284 of the test dropouts, with a recall of 0.511.

# Discussion

The five enrollment predictors helped distinguish later academic outcomes, particularly graduation. Table 6 shows that the model’s test F1 score was highest for graduates (0.663) and lowest for students still enrolled (0.356). The training data give some context for that difference. Students who later dropped out and those still enrolled had the same median admission grade, 124.2 out of 200 (@fig-entry). Informatics Engineering and Evening Management also had similar dropout shares but different shares of students still studying (@fig-programs). We expected program to offer some information and admission grade alone to leave considerable uncertainty. The test results fit that expectation, although this analysis did not isolate the contribution of either predictor.

For an adviser, the two directions of error have different consequences. Of the 284 students who dropped out, the model classified 85 as still enrolled and 54 as graduates (@fig-confusion). All 139 could miss an offer of support if outreach depended on a dropout prediction. In the other direction, 98 students who graduated would have received a dropout flag. The overlap in admission grades offers one plausible reason why future graduates can resemble students who leave. The confusion matrix shows how often this happened, but it cannot tell us why a particular student received that prediction.

The tuned model’s average training and validation macro F1 scores were close (0.529 and 0.522, Table 4), and its held-out score was 0.509. This small gap gives little evidence of severe overfitting within this cohort. The five predictors may carry limited information about events that occur after enrollment, or logistic regression may miss relationships among them. We also assumed scholarship status was known when the student enrolled. An award recorded later would give the model information an adviser did not yet have. All records came from one institution, so performance at another institution remains an open question.

A follow-up could verify scholarship award dates, add prior qualification and its grade, and compare logistic regression with a tree-based model that can capture differences across programs and entry routes. A separate question is how an adviser should use the estimated dropout probabilities. On a later cohort, we could test whether students assigned similar probabilities actually drop out at similar rates. We could then compare how many students an advising team could contact at different thresholds, how many dropouts it would reach, and how many it would miss.
